Jeroham
je-rō'ham
n. (a recurring name in the registers; chiefly the grandfather of Elkanah and so an ancestor of Samuel the prophet)
From Hebrew Yerocham, “he is pitied” or “he findeth mercy”, from racham, to have compassion. It is a passive form: the man does not show mercy, he receives it.

Biblical Definition

Jeroham is a name the registers keep bringing back, and its most consequential bearer stands three generations above one of the great men of the Old Testament. The opening verse of 1 Samuel gives the pedigree: “there was a certain man of Ramathaimzophim, of mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephrathite” (1Sa 1:1), and the Chronicler confirms the Levitical descent, “Eliab his son, Jeroham his son, Elkanah his son” (1Ch 6:27). Elkanah was Hannah's husband; the son she wept for at Shiloh was Samuel. Nothing whatever is recorded of Jeroham himself. Other men of the name appear among the heads of houses in Jerusalem after the return (1Ch 9:12), among the archers who came to David at Ziklag (1Ch 12:7), and as father of one of the five captains Jehoiada took into covenant with him when he brought the boy Joash out of hiding and crowned him in the temple: “Azariah the son of Jeroham” (2Ch 23:1). A name meaning “he findeth mercy”, appearing in the ancestry of the prophet who anointed the first two kings of Israel.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Jeroham; in sacred history it is the name of several men, chiefly the grandfather of Elkanah and ancestor of Samuel.

expand to see more

JEROHAM, n. The name signifies he is pitied, or findeth mercy.

The father of Elkanah, and grandfather of Samuel the prophet.

The Chronicler places him in the Levitical line of Kohath.

A Benjamite of the name is reckoned among the heads of the fathers dwelling at Jerusalem.

Azariah the son of Jeroham was one of the captains taken into covenant by Jehoiada the priest.

Key Scripture

1Sa 1:1 — "Now there was a certain man of Ramathaimzophim, of mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephrathite:"

1Ch 6:27 — "Eliab his son, Jeroham his son, Elkanah his son."

1Ch 9:12 — "And Adaiah the son of Jeroham, the son of Pashur, the son of Malchijah, and Maasiai the son of Adiel, the son of Jahzerah, the son of Meshullam, the son of Meshillemith, the son of Immer;"

2Ch 23:1 — "And in the seventh year Jehoiada strengthened himself, and took the captains of hundreds, Azariah the son of Jeroham, and Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, and Azariah the son of Obed, and Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri, into covenant with him."

Modern Corruption

There is no significant modern redefinition of this name. The principle to recover is that God ordinarily prepares great deliverances through unremarkable households nobody was watching.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Jeroham is a name in a pedigree. What the pedigree does is worth pausing over: it opens the book of Samuel, which is to say it opens the history of Israel's monarchy, and it opens with a hill-country household of no importance. Four generations are named and not one of them is famous. Then a barren woman prays at Shiloh, is taken for a drunkard by a failing priest, and bears the man who will anoint Saul and David. The New Testament opens the same way, with a genealogy and then a village carpenter's betrothed.

The principle to recover is that God's public works are prepared in private and in obscurity. “God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27), and the pattern holds so consistently that it must be deliberate. Samuel came out of a quarrelling polygamous household in the hills; David from the sheepfold; the apostles from fishing boats. Christians are perennially tempted to look for the next work of God among the visible and the credentialed. The registers suggest looking instead at the sort of home Jeroham kept: unremarkable, unrecorded, and three generations upstream of a prophet.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yerocham (H3395), Jeroham, he findeth mercy; racham (H7355), to have compassion; 'Elqanah (H511), Elkanah; sha'al (H7592), to ask; toledoth (H8435), generations.

expand to see more

Hebrew Yerocham (H3395) — Jeroham; he is pitied, he findeth mercy.

Hebrew racham (H7355) — to have compassion, love deeply; the root of the name.

Hebrew 'Elqanah (H511) — Elkanah; his son, the father of Samuel.

Hebrew sha'al (H7592) — to ask; the verb behind Samuel, asked of the LORD.

Hebrew toledoth (H8435) — generations; the register form that preserves such names.

Usage

"“Elkanah, the son of Jeroham” — two generations above the prophet who anointed kings."

"“Azariah the son of Jeroham” — a captain in the covenant that crowned Joash."

"A name meaning “he findeth mercy”, kept in the registers and nowhere else."
